author: Russell Brand
description:
Fauci claims on camera he never sought to censor anyone and doesn't even know who tried to censor Jay Bhattacharya over the Great Barrington Declaration, insisting he simply disagreed with the science. Freedom of Information Act requests tell a different story, showing Fauci himself called for a quick and devastating takedown of Bhattacharya's declaration, the exact censorship campaign he's denying involvement in on live television. Bhattacharya has since gone on to become NIH Director. Russell's panel doesn't hold back, calling the contradiction extraordinary and asking the obvious follow up question, what else has Fauci been lying about.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell breaks down the Telegraph's reporting on how BBC News edited Donald Trump's January 6th speech, splicing together two separate clips recorded 54 minutes apart to make it sound like he directly told supporters to riot, when he never actually said that at all. He plays the real BBC clip alongside the explanation of how it was assembled, calling it a massive reorganization of Trump's actual intention designed to create a false impression. His pointed conclusion, media bias has become so deep and normalized that even the people responsible for it may not fully recognize what they're doing anymore. A sharp, well sourced breakdown of a real and significant editing controversy.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell and his guest argue that each of us is living in our own version of the Garden of Eden right now, whether we realize it or not, and that the serpent's temptation isn't something that happened once, it's happening constantly in your own mind, whatever your personal version of "look at that, that's attractive" might be. They dig into the real cost of walking with God, obedience, and land on a pointed claim about culture itself, that it exists specifically to pull you away from that. A thought provoking reframe on temptation, consciousness, and what it actually means to stay close to God.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell gets candid about the culture he was once part of, one he now describes as broken and, in his words, somewhat diabolical, a world he says was captured by a kind of relentless pursuit of pleasure that people around him celebrated without question. He reflects on how that culture normalized a kind of fame driven exploitation he doesn't stand behind today, sleeping with people who wanted to be with him simply because he was famous, something he now calls no way to live. He's honest about being a flawed man and a sinner, but roots everything he now believes about truth, integrity, and accountability directly in his faith. A genuinely reflective moment on how far removed he feels from the person that culture shaped him into.

author: Russell Brand
description:
Russell makes a sharp case that the exact accusation thrown at independent media, that it's untrustworthy misinformation, is actually far more true of centralized, nationalized media, whether that's the BBC, Chinese state media, or Russian state media. He argues independent media, by its scattered, competing nature, lets people aggregate something closer to the truth, which is exactly why traditional newspapers and broadcast news are struggling right now. His sharpest line lands hard, that centralized media's real function has always been to control and spellbind, selling you products while keeping you obedient and complacent. Russell's own stated goal as part of independent media is the opposite, waking people up and encouraging a kind of rebellion against man made systems, in devotion to God instead. A pointed, unapologetic breakdown of who actually benefits from you staying asleep.
